title: Rachel and Leah (Genesis 29:1–30)
hook: seven years feel like a few days for love, then the deceiver is deceived

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bethel: a stone pillow, a stairway, and a runaway who woke saying God was here and I didn't know.
screen: `GOD WAS HERE AND I DIDN'T KNOW.`

segments.voice: Jacob reaches a well in the east. Shepherds stand around it, waiting, because the stone over its mouth is too heavy to move until all the flocks gather. Then a young woman walks up with her father's sheep. Her name is Rachel, and she is his cousin. Jacob, who has walked for days, rolls the stone off by himself, waters her flock, kisses her, and bursts into tears. Her father Laban takes him in. After a month, Laban asks what wages he wants. Jacob already knows. Not money. Rachel.
screen: `A STONE ON A WELL.` → `RACHEL AND HER SHEEP.` → `JACOB WEEPS.`

segments.voice: Jacob offers seven years of work for her. In the King James Bible: "Jacob served seven years for Rachel; and they seemed unto him but a few days, for the love he had to her." Love does strange things to a clock. Then the wedding night. In the dark, the bride is not Rachel. Laban has sent in her older sister, Leah. In the morning, the man who wore goat skins to fool his blind father finds out what it is to be fooled. "What is this thou hast done unto me?" Laban's answer is cool: in our country we don't give the younger before the firstborn. That's exactly what Jacob did to Esau. Genesis never says the word payback. It lets you hear it. Jacob marries Rachel a week later, and works seven more years. But don't skip Leah. The text says Jacob loved Rachel more, and that God saw Leah was unloved. Her sons get names full of her hope that her husband will finally love her. One of them is Judah. From Judah's line come King David and, in Matthew's family tree, Jesus. The woman Jacob didn't choose is not forgotten by the story. Read honestly, this is a hurting family, not a model marriage: two sisters, one husband, a father who uses them both. The love is real, and so is the pain.
screen: `SEVEN YEARS, LIKE A FEW DAYS.` · `THE DECEIVER IS DECEIVED.` · `THE YOUNGER BEFORE THE FIRSTBORN.` · `LEAH IS SEEN.` · then, large: `FOR THE LOVE HE HAD TO HER.`

segments.voice: Remember a stretch of life that should have felt long: caring for a parent, a long-distance year, a hard job taken for someone else's sake, a baby who wouldn't sleep. Recall how the time actually felt, and who you were doing it for, the long and the light of it together. If you pray, you can give thanks for the person who made it feel short.
Rachel. Hebrew for a ewe, fitting for a shepherdess: the sister Jacob loved at first sight, after serving seven years that felt like a few days.
Your line: love shortens the years. Seven of them felt like a few days. Day three hundred sixty-three, in the books.

howItsDone: Genesis 29:20 is sometimes read at weddings and anniversaries, and Rachel and Leah are remembered in Christian and Jewish tradition as mothers of Israel; Ruth 4:11 names them together in a blessing.

chat.says: Jacob worked fourteen years for Rachel? That sounds romantic. Was it?
options: Partly: the love was real, but Leah was unloved, and Laban used both his daughters.
Yes, a model marriage: one man, one wife, and a happy ending for everyone.
No, Jacob never loved Rachel; he only married her to please his uncle Laban.
chat.meaning: Seven years felt like a few days for love of Rachel, but the text also sees Leah, unloved: a hurting family, not a model marriage.

Laban.meaning: Rachel and Leah's father, Jacob's uncle

Leah.meaning: Rachel's older sister, given to Jacob in the dark

Judah.meaning: Leah's son, from whose line came King David

Matthew.meaning: the Gospel whose family tree runs through Judah to Jesus

notes: The second seven years: Genesis 29:27–30 has Jacob marry Rachel after Leah's bridal week, then serve seven more years. The script says he 'works seven more years and marries Rachel too' and the fork reveal gives the order; confirm.
Genesis 29:31 (KJV 'Leah was hated') paraphrased as 'unloved', which matches the sense of 'loved less' in 29:30; confirm.
Leah's sons' names and her hope of her husband's love (29:32–35) paraphrased; Judah's name is tied to praise in 29:35.
Rachel = 'ewe' is the standard lexicon meaning; confirm.
